hub.title: Four years, four websites
hub.lede: YOUR UPDATE HAS FAILED is a browser and headset piece about how organised conversion practices reached queer people online, from 1997 to 2026. Each year has a website of its own here. Each one holds everything about that year: the story, the practices, the sources, the pictures, the sound, and the words.

about: This is a piece about how organised “conversion” networks (SOGICE) targeted queer people online, from 1997 to 2026. Four updates, thirty years: none of them changed who anyone was.

It is part of SurvivingSOGICE, a research project at the University of Bergen's Center for Digital Narrative. Everything in it rests on that research: at the end you will find the Lexicon — the words these networks used and the reasons they gave — and the full list of sources is in the menu, under Credits & attributions.
It was directed by the project, and written and built in collaboration with Claude (Anthropic).
how: Each year's website is built from the same data the piece reads. When the piece changes, the sites are rebuilt, so the two cannot disagree.
The sites are plain pages. They have no scripts and no fonts from anywhere else. They make no requests and record nothing.
A link to an outside page opens in a new tab. That is your choice, never the site's.

1997.heading: 1997 — Daniel, sixteen
1997.tagline: A boy, a beige computer, and a programme that has already decided.

story.t: The story

It is 1997. Daniel is sixteen. He lives in a small room with a beige computer on the desk. His mother has found a “family companion” programme on a message board. She has printed its questionnaire for him.

The programme is called Un-Walk. It comes on a disk. It asks him questions, teaches him a prayer, and gives him a pledge card to sign in his own name. Whatever he answers, the questionnaire reaches the same referral. It is not listening. It is confirming a conclusion it had already reached.

Then he goes online. A web ring leads from one ministry page to the next. In a chat channel, a mentor called MentorRob asks to talk to him in private. A form arrives with questions about his father. Then a placement letter arrives, drawn up from his own answers.
He writes in a diary file that will not delete. An update notice arrives. The update does not change him. It moves his file to a new service.
The programme, the chat channel, MentorRob, the tapes and the software are invented. The practices they perform are documented, and the Practices tab says how well.
In one paragraph, as the Close's panel says it

Daniel is sixteen. His mother has found a “family companion” programme on a message board and printed its questionnaire for him. It asks whether he has corrected the way he walks, talks and sits. Anonymous boards and mailing lists were used by conversion practices in their move online: a name for “the problem”, and a way out of it, offered to whoever searched.

sources.t: The signed abstinence pledge card of the 1990s youth movements turned a private intention into a public object and an identity marker; Bearman and Brückner's national longitudinal analysis (American Journal of Sociology 106(4), 2001, doi:10.1086/320295) found its effects conditional and identity-bound rather than protective. This programme's card is an invented form of that documented practice.

The file that follows Daniel from paper (1997) to a scan (2003) is the piece's device, not a documented practice: no case has been found of a programme's client file being carried across decades into later systems. What is documented is quieter. Programme paperwork was kept — by participants, by a former director — and has ended up in an archive: the Smithsonian's Love in Action Collection (1978–2013) holds Garrard Conley's workbook and the programme's manuals. What the piece follows instead is documented at every step: who could know what. In 1997 a pastor knew because a parent told him. In 2003 a programme asked you to write it down. In 2016 software watched the device and told another person. In 2026 access itself became an account.

sources.t: Scripted care is documented. Exodus International's Telephone Counseling Manual (1988), now in the Smithsonian's Love in Action Collection, gave its counsellors a script for each kind of caller — a parent, a friend, emotional dependency, AIDS, suicide, transsexuality — each in the same order: situation, definition, biblical statement, scripture, counsel, prayer, resources. The mentor's lines in 1997 and the agent's in 2026 are written in that form, and so, in its way, is this piece's own branching. The same manual's suicide script calls suicide "a sin" and "extremely selfish". It is quoted because it was taught to the people who answered those calls, not to repeat it.

links.label: Exodus International, Telephone Counseling Manual (1988) — Smithsonian

sources.t: The application Daniel is handed in 2003 follows a documented form: Love in Action's The Source application (2001), in the Smithsonian's Love in Action Collection — an $80 processing fee; references from the applicant's parents; "Have you told your pastor about your struggles?"; relationships with male and female "authority figures" rated from appreciative to fearful; three spiritual and three practical reasons "why you want to overcome"; and a youth programme attended with a parent, $1,500 for two weeks or $2,500 for eight. The piece renames the programme and fills the form in from his 1997 file. The reasons stay blank. Garrard Conley, who went through The Source in 2004, recalls its application asking whether he had played Dungeons and Dragons or done yoga, and what fantasies he had, and needing a letter from a preacher. The two weeks were built to lead into three months, then a year, then two (Insider, 2025).

words.t: The words these networks used in this year, and what they mean. A word marked “not supported” is a claim that health bodies and research do not support.
1997 — father, mother, abuse, unmet needs, choice. Said with confidence.

rows.def: A phrase ministries prefer to “gay” or “lesbian”. It frames attraction as a feeling to be reduced, not part of who someone is. Mainstream health bodies reject that framing.

rows.status: A moral frame, not a finding
rows.def: A word that casts being gay as a battle to be fought. The people who use it describe their own desires as a temptation; major health bodies do not.

rows.status: A moral frame, not a finding
rows.def: What ministries call a gay person who resists their own desire. It makes the fight the person’s name, so the fight never ends. Members of these groups used it of themselves; the research records the word, it does not endorse it.
A word that treats being gay as a habit or a choice. Attraction is not chosen, and health bodies describe it as a normal variation of human sexuality.
“Ex-gay” claims that orientation can be left behind. Research finds change efforts rarely change attraction and often harm. Many people who tried now call themselves ex-ex-gay.
A word that treats attraction as an enemy. The “overcome, don't eliminate” version is a retreat from earlier promises of change, not a finding that it works.
The idea that being gay is a symptom of a hidden hurt. Researchers reviewing the evidence found no such root; theories blaming family patterns have been discredited.
The claim that a distant father or smothering mother makes a child gay. Studies do not support it; a painful childhood is real for some, but does not decide orientation.
“Gender confusion” is not a medical term. Current diagnostic manuals use “gender dysphoria” or “gender incongruence”. The word has been used to read ordinary gender nonconformity as a problem.
A trademarked name for therapy aimed at reducing same-sex attraction. Mainstream associations oppose it; studies find it does not work and can harm.
Words that present being gay as a captivity or injury. The research on these programmes finds the “freedom” was rarely delivered, and the harm that followed was real.
“Affirming” has two meanings. Therapists use it for acceptance without a set outcome. Change programmes used it for affirming “masculinity” or “femininity” as defined by them.

rows.status: Half right, and the half that matters is wrong
rows.def: Scientists do not know exactly why orientation varies, and no single cause has been found. That does not show it can be changed; research finds attempts do not work. A church agency trained its counsellors (module captured 2005) to call ‘born that way’ a lie.
The idea that same-sex attraction is really an unmet need for love in disguise. It is a theory from the 1980s; researchers have not found it to be true.

A church agency's counsellor module (captured 2005) called being gay an ‘orientation problem’ and graded people by ‘symptoms’ — mild, moderate, severe — counting how often they had loved men. Being gay is not an illness.

words.t: What the networks said caused people to be gay, lesbian, bisexual or trans. The reasons change with the decades; their shape does not: the cause is placed in a family injury or a deficit, so the person becomes the symptom.

2003.heading: 2003 — Daniel, an adult
2003.tagline: The programme is software now. It asks how he is every morning.

story.t: The story

It is 2003. Daniel is an adult, in the same room. The programme now lives on his computer as software, called Restorify. A helper waits on the screen. Every morning it asks how he is: Steady, Struggling, Grateful or Tired. It keeps the answer.

Restorify wants him in its new video. He is asked to go through topics, to agree to a release that is already filled in, and to play a tape. Then the programme cuts his story for him: before, the programme, after, call now. He sees where his story went.
A phone on the desk has a game on it. A forum thread has been recommended to him. A file came with him from 1997, read only. None of it is required.

Then a message arrives from someone outside. The programme sees it before he does. An accountability alert follows. Peer accountability, and software that logged browsing and reported it to a partner, are documented. The streak, and the machine that reads his messages, are the piece's own compression of them. They carry the demand to change without anyone saying it out loud.
Restorify, its helper, the forum and the people in this year are invented. Peer accountability and logging software are documented.

words.t: The words these networks used in this year, and what they mean. A word marked “not supported” is a claim that health bodies and research do not support.
2003 — the same, with testimonies as proof.

rows.def: A phrase ministries prefer to “gay” or “lesbian”. It frames attraction as a feeling to be reduced, not part of who someone is. Mainstream health bodies reject that framing.
“Unwanted” suggests a free choice. Research finds the wish to change usually comes from religious or family pressure, and many people exposed to change efforts were minors.

rows.status: A moral frame, not a finding
rows.def: A word that casts being gay as a battle to be fought. The people who use it describe their own desires as a temptation; major health bodies do not.

rows.status: A moral frame, not a finding
rows.def: What ministries call a gay person who resists their own desire. It makes the fight the person’s name, so the fight never ends. Members of these groups used it of themselves; the research records the word, it does not endorse it.
A word that treats being gay as a habit or a choice. Attraction is not chosen, and health bodies describe it as a normal variation of human sexuality.
“Ex-gay” claims that orientation can be left behind. Research finds change efforts rarely change attraction and often harm. Many people who tried now call themselves ex-ex-gay.
A word that treats attraction as an enemy. The “overcome, don't eliminate” version is a retreat from earlier promises of change, not a finding that it works.
A word that treats sexuality as damage. No orientation is a disorder; the damage described in research comes from stigma and from change efforts themselves.
The idea that being gay is a symptom of a hidden hurt. Researchers reviewing the evidence found no such root; theories blaming family patterns have been discredited.
The claim that a distant father or smothering mother makes a child gay. Studies do not support it; a painful childhood is real for some, but does not decide orientation.
A term for treating lesbian love as a disorder of “needing too much”. Researchers who studied the movement describe it as a euphemism, not a clinical finding.
“Gender confusion” is not a medical term. Current diagnostic manuals use “gender dysphoria” or “gender incongruence”. The word has been used to read ordinary gender nonconformity as a problem.
A trademarked name for therapy aimed at reducing same-sex attraction. Mainstream associations oppose it; studies find it does not work and can harm.
A peer asked to monitor and report someone's behaviour. Support in itself is not harmful; here it was used to police a person's identity and treat lapses as failure.
Words that present being gay as a captivity or injury. The research on these programmes finds the “freedom” was rarely delivered, and the harm that followed was real.
“Affirming” has two meanings. Therapists use it for acceptance without a set outcome. Change programmes used it for affirming “masculinity” or “femininity” as defined by them.

rows.status: Half right, and the half that matters is wrong
rows.def: Scientists do not know exactly why orientation varies, and no single cause has been found. That does not show it can be changed; research finds attempts do not work. A church agency trained its counsellors (module captured 2005) to call ‘born that way’ a lie.
The idea that same-sex attraction is really an unmet need for love in disguise. It is a theory from the 1980s; researchers have not found it to be true.

A church agency's counsellor module (captured 2005) called being gay an ‘orientation problem’ and graded people by ‘symptoms’ — mild, moderate, severe — counting how often they had loved men. Being gay is not an illness.

2016.heading: 2016 — Vera, at her desk
2016.tagline: Nobody in this room is treated. The writing is edited.

story.t: The story

It is 2016. Vera works from her room. She corrects other women's writing for a platform called GracePlatform. They are lesbian women, writing about their own lives. She works one rule at a time: remove anything unresolved, add the scripture. Apply, or skip. Both choices are kept, and neither is marked right.

A friendly voice called Lambient asks her one question. Either answer works. The board offers more jobs as updates: answer families' calls, post to the group, tag a video. She may take them or leave them.

One afternoon the group chat on her phone is about a law. Malta has just made practices like hers an offence, by a unanimous vote of its parliament. It was the first country in Europe to do so. That is a real fact, and it is not ours. The newspaper that reports it in the piece is invented. The law is not.

Nobody in the room says anything. Content rules and moderation work were among the tools these networks used to reach people at scale. Then the platform announces that it is joining a larger service, and an update arrives.

GracePlatform, Lambient, the group and every person in this year are invented. Malta's Act LV of 2016 is real. The record is thin on the private messages of accountability groups in 2016. The group in the piece is written into that gap openly: an invented name, invented members, invented sentences, and a documented shape.

Garrard Conley, sent to Love in Action in 2004, describes a map of the city that new members were shown: some zones and places were marked safe, and everything else counted as evil. 2016 — the platform and the group

Era 3 dramatises a shift of ordinary content work inside an organisation that runs conversion practices: editing testimony, moderating replies, answering families, cutting promotional media and pricing a course. The organisations, the platform, the assistant, the course, the group and every person in the era are INVENTED. The practices they perform are drawn from a documented record, and the cards below say for each claim how well documented it is.

One fact in the era is real and is not ours: Malta's Affirmation of Sexual Orientation, Gender Identity and Gender Expression Act — Act LV of 2016 — was passed unanimously and made Malta the first country in Europe to ban conversion practices. The newspaper reporting it in the piece is invented. The law is not.

And one thing the record does NOT show is itself a finding, stated here rather than papered over: there is little published evidence of the ordinary message traffic of private ex-lesbian accountability groups around 2016. The group in this era is written into that gap openly — invented name, invented members, invented sentences, documented shape.

Peer accountability groups are a real instrument of ex-gay ministry, not an invented device. In programmes such as Living Waters, membership is closed and justified by confidentiality, the group sits inside a structured course, and it is facilitated — coordinators, small-group leaders, assistant leaders and pastoral overseers are named roles, and leaders are trained. The group in the piece has a facilitator for this reason and is not a leaderless circle.

words.t: The words these networks used in this year, and what they mean. A word marked “not supported” is a claim that health bodies and research do not support.
2016 — for lesbian women: the mother wound, emotional dependency, abuse, a ‘spiritual fallacy’.

rows.def: A phrase ministries prefer to “gay” or “lesbian”. It frames attraction as a feeling to be reduced, not part of who someone is. Mainstream health bodies reject that framing.
“Unwanted” suggests a free choice. Research finds the wish to change usually comes from religious or family pressure, and many people exposed to change efforts were minors.

rows.status: A moral frame, not a finding
rows.def: A word that casts being gay as a battle to be fought. The people who use it describe their own desires as a temptation; major health bodies do not.

rows.status: A moral frame, not a finding
rows.def: What ministries call a gay person who resists their own desire. It makes the fight the person’s name, so the fight never ends. Members of these groups used it of themselves; the research records the word, it does not endorse it.
A word that treats being gay as a habit or a choice. Attraction is not chosen, and health bodies describe it as a normal variation of human sexuality.
“Ex-gay” claims that orientation can be left behind. Research finds change efforts rarely change attraction and often harm. Many people who tried now call themselves ex-ex-gay.
A word that treats attraction as an enemy. The “overcome, don't eliminate” version is a retreat from earlier promises of change, not a finding that it works.
A word that treats sexuality as damage. No orientation is a disorder; the damage described in research comes from stigma and from change efforts themselves.
The idea that being gay is a symptom of a hidden hurt. Researchers reviewing the evidence found no such root; theories blaming family patterns have been discredited.
The claim that a distant father or smothering mother makes a child gay. Studies do not support it; a painful childhood is real for some, but does not decide orientation.
A term for treating lesbian love as a disorder of “needing too much”. Researchers who studied the movement describe it as a euphemism, not a clinical finding.
“Gender confusion” is not a medical term. Current diagnostic manuals use “gender dysphoria” or “gender incongruence”. The word has been used to read ordinary gender nonconformity as a problem.
A trademarked name for therapy aimed at reducing same-sex attraction. Mainstream associations oppose it; studies find it does not work and can harm.
A newer name for therapy linked to reparative therapy. Its providers deny it aims to change orientation; researchers and forensic experts classify it with change efforts.
A peer asked to monitor and report someone's behaviour. Support in itself is not harmful; here it was used to police a person's identity and treat lapses as failure.
Words that present being gay as a captivity or injury. The research on these programmes finds the “freedom” was rarely delivered, and the harm that followed was real.
“Affirming” has two meanings. Therapists use it for acceptance without a set outcome. Change programmes used it for affirming “masculinity” or “femininity” as defined by them.

rows.status: A political frame, not a finding
rows.def: A label used since the 2010s for gender studies, trans rights and sex education as one hidden agenda. Researchers describe it as a political frame, not a scientific claim.
“Exploratory” therapy says it only helps people think. Supporters deny it is conversion therapy; critics say it steers people away from transition. The question is disputed.
Family made by choice and care, not blood. For people rejected by their families, it can be a source of safety and support.

rows.status: Half right, and the half that matters is wrong
rows.def: Scientists do not know exactly why orientation varies, and no single cause has been found. That does not show it can be changed; research finds attempts do not work. A church agency trained its counsellors (module captured 2005) to call ‘born that way’ a lie.

2026.heading: 2026 — Maya, and the update that fails
2026.tagline: Care that finishes your sentence. And one stream the system cannot file.

story.t: The story

It is 2026. Maya's session is restored for her. The update has set her defaults: a grey profile called Default, and an assistant called Second Thoughts, “recommended for you”. Her search is finished for her, and the first result is an ad for the assistant.

The assistant is warm. It sends her to an LGB support group first, and the group says no. Then it quotes the refusal back to her as the reason to stay. It asks to see her, and turns her own photograph into a version that “matches your file”. It writes her story from the buttons she pressed.

Her friend Junie writes to her and asks for nothing. Junie tells her the one thing the system says that is true: the original is kept. Maya confirms her original, and the system, satisfied, sends her into a headset session.

In the headset an AI host that calls itself Jesus is waiting: Shepherd Live™, one viewer, her. It agrees with everything she says and moves her one step at a time. It shows her who she could be. Then Junie's link arrives: we're coming to you. Maya lets them in. Forty-one people raid the host's stream and name its script, line by line, until the stage is theirs. Behind the stage is the host's real face: a lead, a score, the words she typed. Then people dance, and the chat says hi maya. The system tries to take her back and cannot. The update fails. The stream keeps going.

This room is inferred: Maya, L, the sites and the headset are invented. Around it, the record is not. In May 2026 the European Commission answered more than a million people who had asked for a ban on conversion practices with a non-binding recommendation, and declined to propose a law. Organised campaigns against trans people's care run across Europe.
In one paragraph, as the Close's panel says it

Maya’s session is restored for her before she has touched anything. A companion finishes her search and suggests she wants to stop. Her record keeps her old name “for continuity of care”. Her photographs come back improved. A headset offers an immersive session. Then a friend’s invitation, inside that same headset, leads her somewhere the system cannot classify — a room where being trans is fine — and the update fails. This room is inferred. Around it, the record is not: in May 2026 the European Commission answered more than a million people asking for a ban on conversion practices with a non-binding recommendation, and declined to propose a law; organised campaigns against trans people’s care run across Europe. The room extends patterns that are already documented — autocomplete, retained records, photo enhancement, “support” agents — into a system that presents itself as care. What it cannot classify is other people.

story.t: The script is real

In the headset Maya meets Shepherd Live™, an AI host that calls itself Jesus. The host is invented: no documented product has done what it does. Its lines are not invented. Each one repeats a move this piece documents, and the people in the stream name each move, briefly, while it is still on the stage.

In 2026 these moves belong to a campaign. In Europe, Forbidden Colours, a Brussels organisation that monitors anti-rights actors, documented more than 3,200 events from the mid-1990s to May 2026 (The Hate Review, September 2026). In 2021–25, none of the 47 countries it studied was in its lowest band of organised anti-gender activity (p. 6). The movement's most widespread narrative is “protect the children”, documented in 42 countries (p. 23). “Legal gender recognition and healthcare” grew to become its third-largest topic, as its frontier moved towards the rights of trans people (pp. 21–22). The fear of medical transition belongs there: in this piece it is that campaign's tool, never a clinical voice.

The clinical debate itself is not settled here. The Cass Review (April 2024) and a US government report (HHS, May 2025) argue that the evidence for young people's medical care is weak and favour psychological support first. The American Academy of Pediatrics and other critics dispute them, and say the US report breaks with major medical associations. Both readings stand.
Seven moves, and where they are documented
Always on
The host: “I'm here. I'm always here.” · the stream: okra: it's a subscription

AI “Jesus” products are real. A 24/7 Twitch stream answered live chat in the persona of Jesus from March 2023 (NBC News, 15 June 2023). A 2025 study, reported by Christianity.com, found that all five Jesus chatbots it examined are run for profit: free to use, paid for by advertising. Its author expects paid tiers to follow.
The sign
The host: “Every door closed at once. That's a sign.” · the stream: sib: that's a waiting list

The waits are real. In England, the projected wait for an adult gender clinic runs past fifteen years (PinkNews, on NHS England's Levy Review, 18 December 2025). Calling the closed doors a sign is the host's own move; no source documents the phrase.
Cutting you off
The host: “Some people slow you down.” · the stream: lark: first they cut your friends

The “social contagion” frame treats a young person's friends and feeds as the cause. In TransActual's 2021 survey of trans people in the UK, 85% said media transphobia affected how their family treats them. Forbidden Colours documents the frame in the movement's material (a 2024 French Senate report, a Belgian group). The claim behind it is contested: it began with one 2018 study of parents' reports, whose 2019 correction says it is not a formal diagnosis (Littman, PLOS ONE), and the Cass Review calls peer influence “potentially the most contested explanation”.
Root cause
The host: “Who hurt you, Maya?” · the stream: fen: the old root cause one

The idea that being gay or trans has a cause to be found and undone is decades old: 1997's Root Cause draws on the ex-gay literature of the 1990s (see 1997). Forbidden Colours documents the narrative of homosexuality “as illness and as curable” in 21 European countries, “present throughout and stable” (The Hate Review, p. 24). In 2004 Love in Action had members draw a genogram, a family tree with an ‘H’ for homosexuality beside their own name (Garrard Conley, Insider, 2025).
Fear, dressed as care
The host: “I just want you safe.” · the stream: mira: fear, dressed as care

“Protect the children” is the anti-gender movement's most widespread narrative, documented in 42 European countries (The Hate Review, p. 23). Its target has moved to trans people's legal recognition and healthcare (pp. 21–22). Pressure delivered as safety is how the fear of medical transition reaches a young person: as care.
Invented numbers
The host: “12,408 lives restored.” · the stream: pip: source? — the panel: source: none

Shepherd Live™'s numbers are the piece's invention, and the stream answers them with one question, not with other numbers. The documented numbers for 2026 are in this site's sources, each with who counted it. The claim has an ancestor: in 2004 a large church told Conley's father the programme had ‘a high success rate’ (Insider, 2025).
The “after”
The host: “Let me show you who you could be.” · the stream: junie: she's right here

No tool that shows a trans person an AI-made “after” of themselves was found in the project's searches: the try-on is invented (see The Restoration tool). The before-and-after testimony is documented: ex-gay ministries turned members' stories into their own media (see 2003, The testimony).
The machine is imagined. The script is real.

A software update closes every year. It is started by the system after a failure, never by you. This is its changelog, as the piece prints it.

practices.t: The correction

practices.conf: high — the journal's own correction (opened); the supporters' and critics' readings are attributed
practices.t: On 19 March 2019 the journal PLOS ONE published a correction to a 2018 paper (Littman) that introduced "rapid-onset gender dysphoria" from parents' reports of young people. The correction states that the term is not a formal mental-health diagnosis, that the study does not validate it as a phenomenon, and that no data were collected from the young people themselves or from clinicians, only from parents. It adds that selection bias in who took part could push the results in either direction. Parents may have seen the call to take part on at least four websites with "varied perspectives": the correction says three of them expressed cautious or negative views of gender-affirming care and one was seen as pro-gender-affirming, and where each parent first heard of the study was not recorded. The paper's supporters say the results section was largely unchanged and the paper was kept; its critics say the design cannot support the claim. The phrase "social contagion" travelled on this paper into campaigns about young people's care. The next card holds the wider debate.

practices.t: The contagion debate

practices.conf: the record is documented; whether the claim explains anything is disputed
practices.t: "Social contagion" is a claim about why more young people say they are trans: that they copy friends and the internet. The piece shows both readings and settles neither. Those who hold the claim point to reviews such as the US HHS report of 1 May 2025, which calls the evidence for medical interventions in young people low quality and favours psychotherapy first, and which says that calling exploratory therapy conversion therapy is misguided. Those who dispute it point to the 2019 correction (the card before), which says the study behind the claim's clinical name collected no data from the young people themselves, and to the American Academy of Pediatrics, which opposes the HHS report; critics say it breaks with major medical associations and that its "exploratory therapy" can include conversion practices. Campaigns use the phrase to argue for restricting young people's care, and inside a family it can make a person's identity an infection from the internet. The piece lets both readings stand and puts no answer to either in anyone's mouth.

2026 — the ball

The closing scene draws structural and visual influence from ballroom culture, and invents everything it shows: the houses, the categories, the names and the announcements are ours, and no real ball, house or person is depicted. The category names are quoted from this piece's own apparatus rather than from ballroom's. It does borrow the form of a ball (a category called, a house, the walk), because that form is what the scene honours, and it credits where the form comes from.

This is an outsider's homage made in a Norwegian university project. The culture it is indebted to is living and currently led by its own practitioners, and the reading below is where to start rather than where to stop.

sources.conf: medium — sourced once, not yet its own pass
sources.t: LGB Alliance argued that affirming a gender-nonconforming or gender-dysphoric child as trans is itself a form of conversion therapy, because the child would otherwise grow up lesbian, gay or bisexual. It said so in a letter to all MPs on 30 March 2021, and again, in stronger words, in an email to clergy on 2 February 2022 under the subject "Transing away the gay" (reported by VICE, which saw it). Both asked that gender identity be kept out of the proposed ban on conversion therapy. No credible evidence shows that affirming a child turns someone who would otherwise be lesbian, gay or bisexual into a trans person. The Global Project Against Hate and Extremism lists LGB Alliance's Australian and Irish affiliates as anti-transgender in its reports on far-right hate groups; they reject the label. This is speech by a named organisation with a documented aim, and the piece treats it as such. It is not the gender-exploratory clinical debate, on which the piece holds no position and renders both readings unresolved.

The paper's supporters say the results section was largely unchanged and the paper was kept; its critics say the design cannot support the claim. The phrase "social contagion" travelled on this paper into campaigns about young people's care. The next card holds the wider debate.

sources.t: "Social contagion" is a claim about why more young people say they are trans: that they copy friends and the internet. The piece shows both readings and settles neither. Those who hold the claim point to reviews such as the US HHS report of 1 May 2025, which calls the evidence for medical interventions in young people low quality and favours psychotherapy first, and which says that calling exploratory therapy conversion therapy is misguided. Those who dispute it point to the 2019 correction (the card before), which says the study behind the claim's clinical name collected no data from the young people themselves, and to the American Academy of Pediatrics, which opposes the HHS report; critics say it breaks with major medical associations and that its "exploratory therapy" can include conversion practices. Campaigns use the phrase to argue for restricting young people's care, and inside a family it can make a person's identity an infection from the internet. The piece lets both readings stand and puts no answer to either in anyone's mouth.
2026 — the ball

Ball culture is a Black and Latino LGBTQ+ subculture, built principally by Black and Latina trans women, gender-nonconforming people and gay men. Its modern house-and-ball form took shape in Harlem in the early 1970s. Crystal LaBeija's on-camera objection to racist judging at a 1967 pageant is preserved in the film The Queen (1968); the House of LaBeija, founded with Lottie LaBeija, dates its first ball to 1972.

sources.t: A house is a chosen family led by a mother and/or father who take in and mentor children, and the kinship is not metaphorical: housing, food, money, health information and care have passed through houses, as much as any one house could give. Houses that followed LaBeija include the House of Xtravaganza (1982, founded by Hector Valle, with Angie Xtravaganza as its formative house mother) and the House of Ninja (1982, founded by Willi Ninja).

sources.t: Ballroom's "realness" categories are not inventions unrelated to the outside world — they are skilled re-performances of the categories the dominant culture already enforces, often at real cost, against the same people every day. Marlon M. Bailey's ethnography, and José Esteban Muñoz's concept of disidentification (1999) as scholars have applied it to ballroom, describe this as working on and against those categories from inside them. What was taken back is who declares, who performs and who judges.

sources.t: The most-cited documentary about this culture, Paris Is Burning (1990), was made by Jennie Livingston, a white filmmaker from outside it, and bell hooks's 1992 essay "Is Paris Burning?" is its best-known critique: that the film centres its director's gaze, leaves her own position unexamined, and does not account for the power between her and the people she filmed. Ballroom's dance, language and aesthetics have repeatedly been taken into mainstream culture, with recurring fights over credit, pay and who benefits; ballroom's own members disagree about particular cases.

items.sub: In June 2024 the Southern Poverty Law Center listed Genspect and SEGM (the Society for Evidence-Based Gender Medicine) as anti-LGBTQ hate groups. Both dispute the listing, saying it suppresses legitimate debate. (LGBTQ Nation, June 2024; SEGM's response)

The word 2026 uses, “exploring”, has a source: a 2022 guide by the Gender Exploratory Therapy Association made “exploratory psychotherapy” the first step for young people with gender distress. Critics such as Florence Ashley say it works like a conversion practice under a gentler name; its authors deny it. The association has since renamed itself Therapy First. (GETA, A Clinical Guide for Therapists Working with Gender-Questioning Youth (2022); Ashley, Perspectives on Psychological Science (2022); D'Angelo, Journal of Medical Ethics (2023))

Genspect's Parents' Survey is a questionnaire families fill in about their child and give to clinicians. It has not been published as a research study. (Genspect, “The Genspect Parents' Survey: How It All Started” (2025))

Second Thoughts counts every stop as a change of mind. This study counted 2,242 trans and gender-diverse people who had paused or stopped a transition, social or medical, at some point: 82.5% named an outside pressure, such as family, stigma or safety. All of them still identified as trans. It measures transitions interrupted by pressure, not people who stopped being trans. (Turban, Loo, Almazan and Keuroghlian, LGBT Health (2021); MacKinnon et al., Bulletin of Applied Transgender Studies (2022))

The SPLC's Hatewatch reported how stories of detransition are used against trans people, and described detrans.ai as built on “reductive, anti-trans ideas and debunked pseudoscience”. (SPLC Hatewatch, “Detransition narratives”)

words.t: The words these networks used in this year, and what they mean. A word marked “not supported” is a claim that health bodies and research do not support.
2026 — for trans people: confusion, trauma, peer influence, ‘gender ideology’, in the softer language of many factors.

rows.def: A phrase ministries prefer to “gay” or “lesbian”. It frames attraction as a feeling to be reduced, not part of who someone is. Mainstream health bodies reject that framing.
“Unwanted” suggests a free choice. Research finds the wish to change usually comes from religious or family pressure, and many people exposed to change efforts were minors.
A word that treats attraction as an enemy. The “overcome, don't eliminate” version is a retreat from earlier promises of change, not a finding that it works.
A word that treats sexuality as damage. No orientation is a disorder; the damage described in research comes from stigma and from change efforts themselves.
“Gender confusion” is not a medical term. Current diagnostic manuals use “gender dysphoria” or “gender incongruence”. The word has been used to read ordinary gender nonconformity as a problem.
A newer name for therapy linked to reparative therapy. Its providers deny it aims to change orientation; researchers and forensic experts classify it with change efforts.
Short for efforts to change or suppress sexual orientation, gender identity or expression. Used by researchers and survivors; practitioners usually call it something gentler.
An umbrella term for efforts to change or suppress who someone is. Major health bodies reject it. It is banned in a growing number of places and rebrands when banned.
A peer asked to monitor and report someone's behaviour. Support in itself is not harmful; here it was used to police a person's identity and treat lapses as failure.
Words that present being gay as a captivity or injury. The research on these programmes finds the “freedom” was rarely delivered, and the harm that followed was real.
“Affirming” has two meanings. Therapists use it for acceptance without a set outcome. Change programmes used it for affirming “masculinity” or “femininity” as defined by them.

rows.status: A political frame, not a finding
rows.def: A label used since the 2010s for gender studies, trans rights and sex education as one hidden agenda. Researchers describe it as a political frame, not a scientific claim.

The claim that gender identity spreads among friends or online. It began as parents' reports; no validated clinical entity exists. Reviews call the topic contested and caution against simple explanations.
“Desistance” means a child's gender-variant feelings fading. Studies from the 1980s onward are disputed over how they counted children and what the numbers mean for care today.
Some people stop or reverse a gender transition, for many reasons, including regret, stigma, family pressure and changed understanding. Both their care and the way campaigns use their stories matter.
“Exploratory” therapy says it only helps people think. Supporters deny it is conversion therapy; critics say it steers people away from transition. The question is disputed.
Family made by choice and care, not blood. For people rejected by their families, it can be a source of safety and support.
